result:
I’ve been thinking about windows.

Not the philosophical kind, though maybe those too. I mean the ordinary rectangles of glass set into walls, the ones we glance through without really seeing. A window is such a simple thing, but it does something almost magical: it turns distance into a picture. It takes a stretch of sky, a tree, a passing stranger, a rooftop, a blinking traffic light, and frames them into something that looks like meaning.

There’s a strange comfort in watching the world through a window. It lets us be present without being exposed. We can see rain sliding down the glass while staying dry. We can watch people hurry past with umbrellas and wonder where they are going, what they are late for, who is waiting for them. A window invites a kind of gentle speculation. It turns everyday life into a quiet story.

I think that’s why so many people love sitting near windows in cafés, trains, and airports. A window seat is not just a place to sit; it is a place to dream. Movement becomes hypnotic. Telephone wires rise and fall. Houses flash by. Clouds rearrange themselves into improbable shapes. Even boredom can become interesting when there is something to look at just beyond reach.

Windows also remind us that there is always somewhere else. From inside a room, no matter how small or familiar, a window says: the world continues. There is weather happening. There are birds arguing in the branches. Someone is carrying groceries home. A dog is sniffing a patch of grass with enormous seriousness. Life is not only what is happening to us in this moment; it is also what is happening around us, beside us, without needing our permission.

Maybe that’s why they matter so much in difficult times. When we feel trapped, tired, or stuck inside our own thoughts, a window can be a small mercy. It doesn’t solve anything. It doesn’t fix the problem. But it offers perspective. It says, look—there is still space. There is still light changing. There is still a horizon, even if only a narrow one between buildings.

I like how windows blur the line between inside and outside. At dusk, when lamps begin to glow and the glass darkens, reflections appear. You see your own face floating over the street, your own room layered onto the world beyond. For a moment, the interior and exterior occupy the same plane. The self and the outside world become translucent to each other. It’s a little eerie, and a little beautiful.

There are also windows we carry with us. Screens, mostly. Phones, laptops, tablets—windows into conversations, memories, arguments, celebrations, other lives. They offer connection, but they can also make us forget the difference between looking and being present. A window can invite curiosity, but it can also become a barrier we hide behind. There is a difference between watching life and avoiding it.

Still, I don’t think the answer is to look away entirely. Maybe the point is to choose our windows more carefully. To look through some that make the world larger instead of smaller. To notice what is real: the smell of air after rain, the sound of leaves, the way afternoon light can turn an ordinary wall golden. To use windows not as escapes, but as reminders.

Reminders that there is more than this one room, this one worry, this one version of the day.

Sometimes, when I can’t sleep or my thoughts feel too loud, I stand by a window at night and just watch. The street below goes about its quiet business. A car passes. A light changes color for no one. The dark isn’t empty; it’s full of small, continuing things. And that helps. It doesn’t fix everything, but it changes the scale of everything. My problems don’t disappear, but they stop filling the entire frame.

Maybe that’s what I like most about windows. They give us distance, but not isolation. They let us see without demanding we participate. They remind us that the world is both intimate and vast, both close enough to touch and far enough to wonder at.

And perhaps that’s enough for one small reflection: to remember that wherever we are, there is usually a window nearby. Sometimes it’s made of glass. Sometimes it’s a conversation, a book, a song, a memory, a question. Sometimes it’s just the act of looking up.

Either way, there is always something to see.
